Revere

/rih-VEER/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Revere means to feel or show deep, respectful admiration for someone or something.

Islanders still revere the retired ferry captain who never lost a boat in forty winters of crossings.

Worked Example

At the chess academy, students whisper when Grandmaster Ilyana walks past the practice boards. They replay her old tournament games move by move, and when she pauses to watch a match, even the cockiest teenagers sit up straighter. They don't fear her — she is famously gentle with beginners — they simply revere her, the way you honor someone whose mastery feels almost beyond reach.

The hushed voices, replayed games, and straightened posture — respect shown through action, without any fear — demonstrate what it looks like to revere someone.

How Revere Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

honor

honor: to regard with great respect

admire

admire: to regard with warm approval

Antonyms

despise

despise: to look down on with contempt

mock

mock: to ridicule or treat with scorn

How Strong Is It? — respect → revere → worship

respect vs. revere

respect vs. revere: To respect someone is to value them; to revere someone adds a layer of awe — admiration so deep it feels almost sacred.

worship vs. revere

worship vs. revere: To worship goes beyond revering — the admired person is treated as divine, which is where healthy respect stops and idol-worship begins.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of revere.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: intensely; again (Latin)

Root — vere

Root — vere: to stand in awe of, to fear respectfully (Latin vereri)

Put it together

Put it together: Revere pairs the intensifying prefix re- with Latin vereri, 'to stand in awe of.' The root survives in reverence, reverend, and its own opposite, irreverent — 'showing no awe.' To revere someone is thus, quite literally, to stand deeply in awe of them: respect intensified until it borders on the sacred, without tipping into worship.

Use the root in a new word: reverence

Use the root in a new word: reverence: The crowd fell silent in reverence as the flag was folded — the noun form of the same Latin root vereri, 'to stand in awe,' that gives us revere.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, warmly positive; a verb of feeling and showing

Revere names the act of feeling or showing deep admiration — a person reveres someone — while venerable (also in this unit) names the quality the admired person or institution has earned through age, wisdom, or achievement, and reputable is a much cooler, more transactional word meaning simply trustworthy and not shady, with no awe in it at all.
